ingredients.name: Pumpkin
ingredients.notes: peeled, deseeded, and cut into 3cm cubes; kabocha or kent pumpkin preferred, skin can be left on if using a thin-skinned variety

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: 1 cup, enough to just cover the pumpkin while it cooks

ingredients.name: Scraped coconut
ingredients.notes: for grinding into a paste with the garlic, chilli, and mustard seeds

ingredients.name: Thick coconut milk
ingredients.notes: added once the pumpkin is tender

ingredients.name: Roasted Sri Lankan curry powder
ingredients.notes: see sl_006 Roasted Sri Lankan Curry Powder; for garnish at the end

steps.instruction: Grind the scraped coconut with the green chillies, mustard seeds, and a little water in a mortar and pestle or small grinder until it forms a smooth, thick paste. Set aside.
In a pan, add the cubed pumpkin, sliced onion, garlic, fenugreek, curry leaves, pandan leaf, and cinnamon stick.
Add the turmeric, unroasted curry powder, and salt. Stir to coat the pumpkin pieces evenly with the spices.

Pour in the water, enough to just cover the pumpkin. Cover and cook over medium heat for 12-15 minutes, until the pumpkin is soft but still holding its shape (not mushy). Check occasionally and add a splash more water if it dries out before the pumpkin is tender.
Once the pumpkin is tender, reduce the heat to low. Add the ground coconut-chilli-mustard paste and the thick coconut milk. Stir gently to avoid breaking up the pumpkin pieces too much.
Let the curry simmer gently on low heat for about 5 minutes, without boiling vigorously, to avoid curdling the coconut milk. Taste and adjust salt.
Remove from heat and sprinkle the roasted curry powder over the top as a final garnish. Serve hot with rice.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against hungrylankan.com, foodcnr.com, and wandercooks.com for ratio and technique consistency
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 5+ independent sources; strong consensus on the ground coconut-mustard-chilli paste as the dish's defining thickener
notes: This entry reflects the everyday household version of pumpkin curry. A well-known variant called 'wattakka kalu pol' (literally 'pumpkin black coconut') uses dry-roasted, blackened grated coconut and rice ground together as the thickener instead of fresh coconut paste, giving a deeper, nuttier, darker curry -- this is considered a more festive or special-occasion version. Pumpkins that are too watery or carving-style are discouraged; sweeter, meatier varieties like kabocha or kent pumpkin give the best texture and flavour. Overcooking will turn the pumpkin mushy, so check tenderness frequently in the final minutes.
